lead: A residual property is the gap between a real-fluid property and its ideal-gas value at the same temperature and pressure. Ideal-gas formulas alone give wrong enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs energy for a real gas; the residual isolates the deviation. Found from an equation of state or a generalized correlation and added to the ideal-gas value, it gives compressor power, throttle effects, heat-exchanger duties and fugacity coefficients. This chapter shows the defining integrals and works them for carbon dioxide with the virial equation.
prereq: You need the exact differentials of fundamental property relations, the Maxwell relation of Maxwell relations, and the compressibility factor Z and the virial equation from the PVT-behaviour chapters.

sections.h3: Definition at fixed T and P

blocks.text: At temperature T and pressure P, a real fluid has molar property M. The ideal gas at the same T and P has molar property M<sup>ig</sup>. The residual property is M<sup>R</sup> = M − M<sup>ig</sup>. M can be V, U, H, S, G or A; the units follow M. The ideal gas at the same T and P is a reference, not a second real state.

blocks.where: M is any molar property at T and P; M<sup>ig</sup> is the ideal-gas value at the same T and P; M<sup>R</sup> is the residual property.

blocks.text: For an ideal gas, U<sup>ig</sup> and H<sup>ig</sup> depend only on T. S<sup>ig</sup> and G<sup>ig</sup> also depend on P, through S<sup>ig</sup>(T,P) = S<sup>ig</sup>(T,P°) − R ln(P/P°) and G<sup>ig</sup> = H<sup>ig</sup> − T S<sup>ig</sup>. The pressure terms cancel in some residuals and remain in others. Every residual property of an ideal gas is zero. As P → 0, H<sup>R</sup>, S<sup>R</sup>, G<sup>R</sup>, A<sup>R</sup> and U<sup>R</sup> tend to zero. V<sup>R</sup> is different: V<sup>R</sup> = (Z − 1)RT/P tends to B, the second virial coefficient, a finite value, because V and V<sup>ig</sup> both diverge while their difference stays finite.

blocks.where: V<sup>R</sup> is residual molar volume (m³/mol); Z = PV/RT is compressibility factor; R = 8.314 J/(mol K); T is temperature (K); P is pressure (Pa).

blocks.text: Negative V<sup>R</sup> means the real gas occupies less volume than the ideal gas at the same T and P. Attractive forces usually cause this at moderate pressure.

For a pure fluid, the fugacity coefficient is φ = f/P, where f is fugacity and P is pressure. Solution thermodynamics develops φ fully. The residual Gibbs energy is tied to it by G<sup>R</sup> = RT ln φ. The integrated form uses the compressibility factor Z = PV/RT.

blocks.where: G<sup>R</sup> is residual molar Gibbs energy (J/mol); R = 8.314 J/(mol K); T is absolute temperature (K); φ is fugacity coefficient; Z = PV/RT; P is pressure (Pa).

blocks.text: At P → 0, (Z − 1)/P tends to a finite limit, the pressure virial coefficient B′, so the integral remains finite. If φ < 1, then ln φ < 0 and G<sup>R</sup> is negative: the real gas has lower Gibbs energy than the ideal gas at that T and P. If φ > 1, G<sup>R</sup> is positive; φ = 1 gives G<sup>R</sup> = 0. This sign check catches many calculation errors. The same integral also gives the fugacity coefficient used in phase equilibrium, in solution thermodynamics and phase equilibria.
At constant T, the fundamental relation for enthalpy gives dH = [V − T(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>] dP. Integrate from zero pressure, where the gas is ideal, to pressure P.

blocks.where: H<sup>R</sup> is residual molar enthalpy (J/mol); V is molar volume (m³/mol); T is temperature (K); (∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> is the temperature derivative of V at constant pressure; P is pressure (Pa).

blocks.text: For an ideal gas, V = RT/P and T(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = RT/P. The bracket is zero, so H<sup>R</sup> = 0, as required. For a cubic equation of state, substitute V(T,P) and integrate. The result is a closed-form departure function.
Entropy follows from dS = −(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> dP at constant T. With M<sup>R</sup> = M − M<sup>ig</sup>, the residual is:

blocks.where: S<sup>R</sup> is residual molar entropy (J/(mol K)); R = 8.314 J/(mol K); P is pressure (Pa); V is molar volume (m³/mol); (∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> is at constant pressure.

blocks.text: The ideal-gas part is R/P, so the integrand vanishes for an ideal gas. The three residuals are consistent through G<sup>R</sup> = H<sup>R</sup> − T S<sup>R</sup>. Cubic equations of state such as van der Waals, Redlich-Kwong and Peng-Robinson supply V(T,P) and its temperature derivative. Generalized correlations use reduced temperature Tr = T/Tc, reduced pressure Pr = P/Pc and acentric factor ω. They tabulate H<sup>R</sup>/RTc and S<sup>R</sup>/R. The values feed compressor power, valve throttling and heat-exchanger duties.

With the two-term virial equation Z = 1 + BP/RT, where B(T) is the second virial coefficient, the integrals close at once: G<sup>R</sup> = BP, H<sup>R</sup> = P(B − T dB/dT) and S<sup>R</sup> = −P dB/dT. For a gas without B data, the Pitzer correlation of Abbott gives BP<sub>c</sub>/RT<sub>c</sub> = B⁰ + ωB¹ with B⁰ = 0.083 − 0.422/T<sub>r</sub><sup>1.6</sup> and B¹ = 0.139 − 0.172/T<sub>r</sub><sup>4.2</sup>, valid at low to moderate reduced pressure.

figure.caption: The worked example for CO<sub>2</sub> at 350 K. The two-term virial equation with the Abbott correlation gives a straight line Z = 1 + BP/RT that runs just above the accurate values; at 20 bar Z = 0.9425 against 0.9404, and the residuals G<sup>R</sup>, H<sup>R</sup> and S<sup>R</sup> follow from B and dB/dT.

examples.question: At 300 K and 50 bar, a pure gas has fugacity coefficient φ = 0.90. Calculate its residual molar Gibbs energy G<sup>R</sup>. Use R = 8.314 J/(mol K).
steps: Write the relation: G<sup>R</sup> = RT ln φ.
examples.answer: G<sup>R</sup> = −262.8 J/mol; the real gas has lower Gibbs energy than the ideal gas at 300 K and 50 bar.
examples.check:
import math
R = 8.314
T = 300.0
phi = 0.90
GR = R * T * math.log(phi)
print(round(GR, 1))

code.code:

R = 8.314
T = 300.0
phi = 0.90
GR = R * T * math.log(phi)
print(round(GR, 1))

examples.question: Find Z, G<sup>R</sup>, H<sup>R</sup>, S<sup>R</sup> and φ for CO<sub>2</sub> at 350 K and 20 bar with the virial equation and the Abbott correlation. Data: T<sub>c</sub> = 304.2 K, P<sub>c</sub> = 73.83 bar, ω = 0.224.
steps: S<sup>R</sup>/R = −P<sub>r</sub>(dB⁰/dT<sub>r</sub> + ω dB¹/dT<sub>r</sub>) = −0.2709 × (0.4687 + 0.0780) = −0.1481, so S<sup>R</sup> = −1.231 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Check: H<sup>R</sup> − TS<sup>R</sup> = −598.4 + 350 × 1.231 = −167.5 J/mol = G<sup>R</sup>. An accurate equation of state for CO<sub>2</sub> gives Z = 0.940, H<sup>R</sup> = −604 J/mol, S<sup>R</sup> = −1.243 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and φ = 0.944, within 1 %.
examples.answer: Z = 0.9425, φ = 0.944, G<sup>R</sup> = −167.5 J/mol, H<sup>R</sup> = −598.4 J/mol, S<sup>R</sup> = −1.231 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

traps: Using the same temperature and volume instead of the same temperature and pressure. Residual properties are defined at the same T and P.
Thinking an ideal gas has nonzero residual enthalpy or entropy at high pressure. Every M<sup>R</sup> for an ideal gas is zero.
Dropping the sign of ln φ. φ < 1 gives negative G<sup>R</sup>; φ > 1 gives positive G<sup>R</sup>.
Forgetting the sign in S<sup>R</sup>. With M<sup>R</sup> = M − M<sup>ig</sup>, write S<sup>R</sup> = ∫₀<sup>P</sup> [R/P − (∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>] dP.
Using bar in V<sup>R</sup> = (Z − 1)RT/P. Convert pressure to Pa so R in J/(mol K) gives m³/mol; 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa.

quiz.q: Define residual property M<sup>R</sup> for a pure fluid.
quiz.a: M<sup>R</sup> = M(T,P) − M<sup>ig</sup>(T,P), at the same temperature T and pressure P. M can be V, U, H, S, G or A.

quiz.q: Why is every residual property of an ideal gas zero?
quiz.a: Because the real-fluid property and the ideal-gas property are then the same at the same T and P; their difference is zero by definition.

quiz.q: At 300 K and 50 bar, Z = 0.90. Calculate V<sup>R</sup> in cm³/mol. Use R = 8.314 J/(mol K), 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa.
Explain why H<sup>R</sup> uses V − T(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> rather than V − V<sup>ig</sup> alone.
quiz.a: At constant T, dH = T dS + V dP and the Maxwell relation gives T dS = −T(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> dP, so dH = [V − T(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>] dP. The integral of V − V<sup>ig</sup> alone is the residual Gibbs energy G<sup>R</sup>, not H<sup>R</sup>: it leaves out the entropy part of the enthalpy change. The bracket still vanishes for an ideal gas, because T(∂V<sup>ig</sup>/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = RT/P = V<sup>ig</sup>; the temperature-slope term carries how molecular attraction changes with temperature.

quiz.q: For φ < 1, what is the sign of G<sup>R</sup>, and what does it mean physically?
quiz.a: ln φ < 0, so G<sup>R</sup> < 0. The real gas has lower Gibbs energy than the ideal gas at the same T and P; it is more stable than the ideal-gas reference by that amount.

beyond: Not for the exam. Process simulators store residual enthalpy and entropy as departure functions for every stream, and compressor vendors use them to get shaft power. Search next for Peng–Robinson departure functions and the Lee–Kesler tables.
